The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is an essential element of the global climate system, yet its variability on timescales longer than those observed remains unsettled.
Recent studies show that transport variability in the lower AMOC limb is maximized on density surfaces well below the density of maximum overturning.
Recent studies show that transport variability in the lower AMOC limb is maximized on density surfaces well below the density of maximum overturning.
To explore the source and impact of this feature, we analyze lower-limb transport variability using climate simulations and observations from the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program.

We find that enhanced variability at select densities reflects transport redistribution within the lower limb and is not strongly linked with local or downstream AMOC variability on monthly to multidecadal timescales.

Furthermore, the strong transport variability in dense waters leaving the Labrador Sea is tightly linked to variability entering the basin, with the opposing inflow and outflow largely canceling in basin-integrated diagnostics.

The study shows that, despite the Labrador Sea forming the final leg of the Atlantic overturning circulation’s subpolar ‘relay’, transport changes originating in the Irminger and Iceland basins exert the strongest downstream influence.

With AMOC changes historically linked to deep water formation on various timescales 2 , 3 , oceanographers have long been interested in the amount of deep water formed in the Labrador, Irminger and Nordic Seas 4 – 8 to understand how variability in each region impacts the AMOC.
Over the past two decades, modelling studies have indicated strong links between Labrador Sea deep convection, density and AMOC variability 7 – 10 .
However, summer hydrographic surveys from the 1990s 11 suggested that the Labrador Sea contributes minimally to NADW volume.

Consistent with these earlier estimates, direct observations from the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP) 12 later revealed that overturning across the eastern OSNAP section (i.e., in the Iceland and Irminger basins) dominates both the mean and monthly variability of subpolar overturning, with minimal contribution from the Labrador Sea 13 .

Consistent with these earlier estimates, direct observations from the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP) 12 later revealed that overturning across the eastern OSNAP section (i.e., in the Iceland and Irminger basins) dominates both the mean and monthly variability of subpolar overturning, with minimal contribution from the Labrador Sea 13 .

Consistent with these earlier estimates, direct observations from the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP) 12 later revealed that overturning across the eastern OSNAP section (i.e., in the Iceland and Irminger basins) dominates both the mean and monthly variability of subpolar overturning, with minimal contribution from the Labrador Sea 13 .
One modelling study 14 attempted to reconcile the discrepancy between OSNAP observations and earlier modelling studies linking AMOC variability to Labrador Sea processes.

On this basis, the authors argued that although the Labrador Sea contributes only weakly to the mean and monthly variability of the AMOC, it may play a disproportionately important role in driving low-frequency variability.

While surface-forced water mass transformation accounts for a substantial fraction of the mean lower-limb transport, its variability explains only part of the AMOC variability on seasonal to interannual timescales, with the remainder arising from basin storage, interior mixing and advective processes 16 .

Together, these studies leave unresolved how transport variability within specific density classes, including the LSW density range, relates to AMOC variability across timescales, and which density-space transport anomalies more effectively capture AMOC variability, both at the OSNAP section and farther downstream.

Here we show that this separation persists from monthly to multidecadal timescales in both climate models and OSNAP observations.
Pronounced dense variability in the western subpolar North Atlantic should therefore not be interpreted as a direct proxy for AMOC strength.
We attribute this weak linkage to substantial transport compensation within the AMOC lower limb.
Decomposition of the transport anomalies indicates that this compensation is driven primarily by changes in layer thickness rather than by compensating flow speed anomalies.

Across the model ensemble, variability in the eastern subpolar basin exhibits stronger correlations with both the OSNAP MOC and the downstream MOC than variability in the western basin across most density classes and timescales.

Across the model ensemble, variability in the eastern subpolar basin exhibits stronger correlations with both the OSNAP MOC and the downstream MOC than variability in the western basin across most density classes and timescales.
This result is consistent with previous studies highlighting the dominant role of the Irminger and Iceland basins in shaping the AMOC mean state and variability 13 , 22 .

This contrast arises because inflow and outflow anomalies are strongly correlated yet opposite in sign, so their lateral integration across the basin leads to partial cancellation, contributing to the weak relationship between basin-integrated western overturning and overall MOC variability.

This framework helps reconcile our results with previous studies emphasizing the importance of Labrador Sea water mass transformation for downstream AMOC variability 15 .
That downstream signal, expressed as AMOC variability at 50°N, is more consistently reflected in the upstream transport anomalies (OE-Out, OW-In, and OW-Out) than in SFWMT.
Thus, although Labrador Sea transformation can modify the dense signal, it does not emerge as the dominant or most robust control on downstream AMOC variability across models.
These conclusions should be interpreted with awareness of the limitation of CMIP6 climate models in the subpolar North Atlantic.
